title: Extract dev into standalone dev-cli repo
body:
Spin the project-scoped dev/e2e process runner (`dev`) out of the agent-tools umbrella (it lived at `lib/agenttools_dev`) into a first-class peer of pm-cli / research-cli / tg-cli, matching their layout (bin shim, install.sh, install-skill, vendored shared lib + drift guard, CI).

## Acceptance
- [ ] dev_cli package with the full CLI ported, `--version` + `install-skill`
- [ ] `--agenttools-dev-probe`/`agenttools-dev` token + `.agenttools-dev` state-dir preserved (wire contracts)
- [ ] agenttools_config vendored under vendor/ + pinned-SHA drift guard + re-sync script + scheduled drift workflow
- [ ] README, AGENTS.md, LICENSE, CI (ruff + pytest matrix + gitleaks)
- [ ] full unit suite ported + green; `dev` reinstalled from the new repo and verified working
- [ ] agent-tools removal PR + any rig registry follow-up

## Why
dev was the last agent CLI still living inside agent-tools instead of its own repo; the CTO ordered the extraction. Standalone means it versions/ships/tests independently like its siblings.

title: Security: command-substitution check bypassable via apostrophe inside double quotes
body:
Carried over from agent-tools verbatim; flagged by the extraction code review.

`_has_shell_substitution` blanks single-quoted regions (`_blank_single_quoted`) before scanning for `$(`, backticks, `<(`. But `_blank_single_quoted` only tracks `'` — it has no notion of double quotes (unlike `_command_segments` / `_has_shell_redirection`, which track both). A lone apostrophe inside a double-quoted word flips the blanker into single-quote mode for the rest of the string and erases everything after it, including a real substitution.

Repro — a `rig.yaml` script value of:
```
npm test "it's fine" $(touch pwned)
```
`_blank_single_quoted` hits the `'` in `it's`, finds no closing `'`, blanks the remainder → `_has_shell_substitution` returns False. `npm` head passes the dev-tool check; `_ensure_lifecycle_command` passes; `_run_shell(shell=True)` executes the substitution. Same shape defeats the check for backticks and `<(...)`, across `dev run`, `dev start`, `dev e2e run`.

## Fix
Make `_blank_single_quoted` (or a shared tokenizer) enter single-quote mode only when the `'` is outside a double-quoted region — `_has_shell_redirection` already has the two-state machine to copy. Red-first test with the string above (nothing in the suite currently mixes quote styles).

## Why P1
It is the command-shape safety boundary that makes `Bash(dev:*)` safe to allowlist. Pre-existing in agent-tools; not fixed during the extraction to keep the port faithful and avoid mid-cutover behavior change.

title: dev shot: capture-measure-attest visual proof that cannot be faked
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The visual-proof gate's contract was 'any file in the marker dir with a recent mtime'. A bare touch satisfied it, so the attestation carried no information: an agent that never opened a browser could pass it, and an agent that captured a blank page could pass it too.

## User impact
Two batches of completed UI work were stalled because the honour-system marker could not be written, while the same mechanism would have happily accepted proof of a blank page. Reviewers cannot trust a green gate, and agents cannot satisfy it honestly.

## Cost of inaction
The gate stays theatre: it blocks honest work at random while providing no actual evidence that anyone looked at the rendered result. UI regressions ship with a passing visual-proof check.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `dev shot <url> --out <path>` captures with a viewport set before open and a scroll sweep, so reveal-on-scroll content is visible before the shutter
- [ ] A degenerate capture (large contiguous blank band, wrong viewport width, near-blank page) is REJECTED with exit code 3 and NO attestation is written
- [ ] The attestation record binds the capture sha256 and the `git diff --cached` sha256, so it cannot be reused for a different change or survive further edits
- [ ] Adversarial tests use two real captures of the same page — one unswept (42% blank band) must be rejected, one swept (4%) must be accepted

## Screenshots

title: dev shot's default scroll step produces captures its own quality gate rejects
body:
## What
The `dev shot` command performs a scroll sweep before capturing so that reveal-on-scroll content has entered the viewport, then judges the resulting capture and refuses to attest to a degenerate one. Its default sweep step is 400px. On a long marketing page that default is too coarse: content gated on scroll never enters the viewport at some offsets, so the capture comes back with a large uniform band and the command's own quality check rejects it. Passing `--sweep-step 150` produced a usable capture of the same page with no other change. The tool is failing its own gate with its own defaults.

## Why (motivation)
A default that makes the tool reject its own output is the most expensive kind of wrong default, because the failure points at the page rather than at the tool. The command already computes the signal it needs to self-correct: it knows the capture is degenerate at the moment it rejects it, so it could lower the step and retry instead of reporting failure. Options worth weighing rather than prescribing one: lower the constant, derive the step from the viewport height, or retry once with a finer step before giving up.

## User impact
An engineer capturing a screenshot of a long page is told the capture failed its quality check, with nothing in the message pointing at the sweep step. They go looking for a rendering bug in a page that renders correctly, and only find the real cause by guessing at a flag. Worse, an engineer who does not notice the rejection can carry a partly-blank image forward as evidence and draw a confident conclusion from a picture that shows nothing.

## Cost of inaction
Every person capturing a long page pays the same investigation cost, and each one rediscovers the `--sweep-step` workaround independently. The failure mode that already occurred on [the Conloca landing page](https://github.com/conloca/landing) — a fidelity comparison measured against a capture that was 52% blank, producing numbers that meant nothing — stays available to anyone who misses the rejection.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Running `dev shot` against a long reveal-gated page with no `--sweep-step` argument produces a capture that passes the command's own quality check.
- [ ] When the quality check rejects a capture, the command's error output names the sweep step that was used, so the reader can tell the tool's configuration apart from a genuinely broken page.
- [ ] The chosen default is justified in `dev shot --help` or in code, rather than being an unexplained constant.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

Closing.

title: dev stop refuses to stop the process that is actually holding the port
body:
## What
Three related problems seen on 2026-09-05/06. First, `dev start` refuses with "Conloca cannot start: port 8787 is already in use. Stop its owning development session first", but the following `dev stop server` refuses back with "pid 24537 is not recognized as a development tool" because the process holding the port is an esbuild service child, and in another case a storybook child, rather than the top-level runner. Second, `dev status server` reports the target running with a log path while `dev logs server` reports "dev target server has no readable log under logs_root". Third, --repo-only is accepted after the subcommand in `dev run --repo-only server` but rejected before it in `dev --repo-only status server`, with no hint about the correct position.

## Why (motivation)
The safe-stop process matcher recognises only the runner it started, not the toolchain children that inherit the listening socket. status and logs resolve the target through different paths. And the repo-only flag is registered on some subparsers only.

## User impact
The agent is told to stop the old dev server, tries the sanctioned command, and is refused. There is no other approved way to free the port, so the work stops there. Alex sees the app never come up and no explanation beyond two commands contradicting each other.

## Cost of inaction
Agents fall back to raw pkill and lsof, which is exactly what dev stop exists to prevent.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] dev stop can stop the toolchain child that holds a port for a target it owns, or explains precisely which process it will not touch and why.
- [ ] dev status and dev logs agree about whether a target has a readable log.
- [ ] The repo-only flag works in one documented position, and the error names that position when it is used in the other.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- Relates to #27: https://github.com/alex-mextner/dev-cli/issues/27

title: dev stop declares success and deletes state before the OS confirms the process exited
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
agent-tools#538 (merged, review-cli#377) already fixed this exact race class for agenttools_service's ServiceManager (dashboard/config-web/tg-ctl), whose Supervisor.stop() now blocks until the pid is confirmed dead and probe_port() catches a stray fd-inheriting child afterward. dev-cli's own _stop_target/_terminate_pid in dev_cli/cli.py never got the equivalent fix: _send_signal() fires SIGTERM and _stop_target() unlinks the state file and prints success in the very next lines, with zero wait, zero retry, and no port probe anywhere in the file (grep for grace/escalat/SIGKILL/confirm/wait_for/poll_for/retry/deadline in dev_cli/cli.py returns nothing). CROSS-LINK NOTE: this is related to, but NOT a duplicate of, https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/issues/155 (closed, refiled as https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/685 ) -- that ticket is a permanent launchd-label detection gap in agenttools_service's Supervisor.status/is_installed (a legacy hand-installed launchd job under an untracked label is never recognized as running, regardless of timing), whereas this ticket is a pure stop-timing race in dev-cli's own PID-file tracking with no launchd involved at all. Same 'status/stop lies about a live process' symptom class, two independent root causes in two independent codebases -- fixing one does not fix the other.

## User impact
An agent (or Alex) that calls 'dev stop target' immediately followed by 'dev status target' or 'dev start target' — the exact sequence the dev-cli docs recommend for restarting a server — can be told the target is not running while the old process is still mid-shutdown and still holding its port. A subsequent 'dev start' then either fails with an opaque port-in-use error from the NEW process, or (if the target has no fixed port) leaves two live copies of the same dev server running side by side, silently doubling that target's memory/CPU footprint.

## Cost of inaction
Every stop-then-start or stop-then-status sequence stays racy; agents keep hitting spurious port-in-use failures or silently accumulate duplicate dev-server processes, which is itself a contributor to the machine-wide swap/OOM pressure tracked in agent-tools#519.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] dev stop does not remove a target's state record (or report success) until the signalled pid is confirmed dead by polling, with a bounded timeout and a SIGKILL escalation on timeout, mirroring agenttools_service.core.Supervisor.stop()'s confirmed-dead contract — proof: ![proof](/tmp/dev-cli27-proof.txt)
- [x] dev status/dev list never reports a target as unqualified 'configured'/'stopped' while the OS process from the just-removed state record could still be alive; a grace-period or port-liveness probe (mirroring agenttools_service.core.ServiceManager.probe_port(), agent-tools#538) closes the gap — proof: ![proof](/tmp/dev-cli27-proof.txt)
- [x] a regression test starts a fake long-lived child that ignores/delays SIGTERM, calls the stop path, and asserts the state record is NOT removed (or a probe still reports the port live) until the child actually exits — proof: ![proof](/tmp/dev-cli27-proof.txt)

## Screenshots
(none)
